issues.issue: The preamble names "ICICI BANK LIMITED, New York Branch (or any of its overseas branches or subsidiaries party hereto)" as Escrow Agent and Account Bank, leaving it uncertain which legal entity holds that office. Branches are not separate legal persons, and the parenthetical does not say how or when a subsidiary becomes the acting agent.

The recitals state Project cost as "currently estimated to be approximately" US$1,097,000,000 and financing of US$530,000,000/US$713,000,000, yet operative provisions treat those figures as fixed thresholds (Section 2.08(b) permits commitment reduction only if Project costs fall below US$1,097,000,000, and the Financial Closure definition requires exactly US$530,000,000). A court could be asked whether the recital's estimate controls the operative tests.

The recital states flatly that "This Term Loan Facility is guaranteed in accordance with the terms of the Guarantee Agreements by" the Parent and EGL, whereas the EGL Guarantee Agreement caps EGL's post-Commercial-Operations-Date liability at $250,000,000 and terminates it on the EGL Guarantee Release Date. The recital's unqualified language can be argued against the limited guarantee actually delivered.

The cross-reference is left incomplete — "Section 2.20(b" — so the definition points to a subsection that is not properly identified. The reader must supply the missing closing reference to know which provision assigns the meaning.

"Any material property or assets" fixes no threshold, so it is not determinable when an acquisition creates an Additional Collateral Date and triggers the Section 5.14 security obligations. "Material" is nowhere defined for this purpose.

The closing condition is ungrammatical — "require a mandatory prepayment ... on the same terms as the required by the Loans" — and it is unclear whether it qualifies only clause (b)(iii) or the whole quotient. The defect changes which debt goes into the denominator of the pro rata share.

The definition of "Additional Obligations" is circular: it defines the term as obligations under the Supplier Financing "in each case to the extent arising in connection with the Additional Obligations." The limiting phrase uses the term being defined, so its outer boundary cannot be fixed from the text.

After enumerating supplemental security documents, control agreements and consents, the definition sweeps in "each other security agreement or other security instrument or document executed and delivered to the reasonable satisfaction of the Security Agent." That open catch-all sits against the enumerated specifics and has no stated limit on what the Security Agent may demand.

Clause (1)(A) makes the inclusion of equity in a Person's net income "subject to the limitations contained in clause (4) below," but clause (4) addresses extraordinary, unusual or nonrecurring gains and losses and contains no limitation on equity income. The internal cross-reference does not match the clause it points to.

Item (f) deducts "bad or doubtful expenses not provided for," a phrase that is not an accounting concept (the standard term is bad or doubtful debts). What must be deducted cannot be determined from the words used.

"Agents" is defined to include the Intercreditor Agent, but under the Intercreditor Agent and Intercreditor Agreement definitions that office exists only "if and when appointed" under an intercreditor agreement that may never be entered into. Provisions addressed to the "Agents" collectively are therefore of uncertain application.

Clause (ii) capitalizes leases that are not Capital Lease Obligations, but the closing sentence says "Attributable Debt" excludes ordinary-course operating leases not required by GAAP to be treated as capital leases. The two sentences cannot both be given full effect for an ordinary-course operating lease.

"Borrowing" is defined to include "an LC Exposure," yet Section 2.03(c) requires that "each Borrowing shall be comprised entirely of Eurodollar Rate Borrowings" and Section 2.04 requires every Borrowing to be requested by a Borrowing Request specifying an Interest Period. An LC Exposure cannot satisfy those requirements, so the definition and Section 2.03(c)/2.04 pull apart.

The clause reads "commercial banks in the Hibbing, Minnesota, New York, New York, and Singapore are authorized or required by law to remain closed" — a grammatical failure that leaves it unclear whether closure in any one of the three centres, or all of them, disqualifies the day. The stray article and the plural verb make the list's operation uncertain.

Cash counts only if held at "reputable banks or financial institutions, acceptable to the Lenders," with no standard governing acceptability and no requirement of reasonableness. The parenthetical in clause (c) is also left unclosed, blurring where the Lien carve-out ends.

"Standalone net profits after taxation" is neither defined nor a GAAP line item, although Section 1.03 requires accounting terms to be construed in accordance with GAAP. The starting figure for the DSCR therefore has no fixed content.

The syntax leaves it unclear whether "certificates of deposit or time deposits with a maturity of less than six (6) months, issued by a commercial bank" is a second, independent category or must also be government-issued or guaranteed. The single "and" joining the two limbs can be read either way.

The deduction of "the lesser of actual maintenance capital expenditures and US$12,500,000" states no period for the cap, although the definition applies "for any period" and the sweep is tested quarterly. Whether the $12,500,000 is an annual or a per-quarter limit is not stated.

The definition counts scheduled repayments of the Loans, Supplier Financing and Permitted Capex Additional Indebtedness only, omitting other Additional Indebtedness permitted by Section 6.01. The enumeration invites an expressio unius argument that other permitted debt service never reduces the sweep.

The clause says only that the Lenders and Upstream Supplier Financing Creditors "shall have the right to receive" the sweep amount; it imposes no express payment obligation on the Borrower. Whether the Borrower is bound to pay, and on what demand, must be gathered from elsewhere.

The defining parenthetical is misplaced: "results in an amount (a \"Second Sweep Period Sweep Amount\") in excess of 1.15" attaches the defined term to the ratio rather than to the fifty-percent product, contrary to the parallel placement in clause (i). Read literally the Second Sweep Period Sweep Amount is a DSCR figure, not a dollar amount.

This clause directs that any shortfall in the Sweep Amount be paid "out of cash in the DSRA," which cannot readily be squared with the DSRA definition and Section 5.15, under which the Borrower must maintain the Required Amount as a debt service reserve. Draining the reserve to fund a voluntary-style sweep works against the reserve obligation.

The clause requires retroactive adjustment of the fourth-quarter Sweep Amount but provides only for "adjustment ... in the distributions with respect to the Sweep Amount for the first fiscal quarter," with no mechanism if the audited results show an overpayment exceeding the next quarter's sweep. Whether any refund is owed is not addressed.

The First Sweep Period runs from nine months after the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date to April 1, 2014, but the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date may be as late as June 30, 2013, leaving a period of a day or two (and none at all if that date slips). Read with the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date definition, the First Sweep Period may be empty.

"Each full fiscal quarter during the applicable Sweep Period" is undefined where the Sweep Period begins mid-quarter (nine months after the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date). Whether the partial opening quarter counts is not stated.

Applying this definition, the Sweep Payment Date for one quarter is itself the Sweep Date for the next under the Sweep Date definition, so the same date carries both characters and the sweep is computed a quarter in arrears. The interlock between the two definitions is not made explicit.

The 49% acquisition trigger cannot be squared with the LLC Pledge Agreement and the Pledged Borrower LLC Interests definition, under which 51% of the Borrower's Equity Interests are pledged to the Security Agent for the Secured Parties. Enforcement of that pledge by transfer to a purchaser would itself produce a Change in Control.

"Collateral" is defined as "any and all \"Collateral\", as defined in any applicable Security Document" — a circular reference that pushes the content of the term entirely into other instruments. Its scope cannot be settled from this Agreement.

The Collateral Account Agreement is described as "established for purposes of the DSRA and the Escrow Account," yet the Insurance and Other Proceeds Account definition and the Net Debt definition refer to the Insurance and Other Proceeds Account and the Unrestricted Account as also being established under it. The stated purpose is narrower than the accounts the document is elsewhere said to govern.

The date turns on certification that "commercial production has commenced," a term nowhere defined and set by no output, duration or quality benchmark. Because the guarantee periods and sweep dates run off this date, its trigger is left to the certifier's judgment.

The definition requires notice to and certification by the "Lenders' Engineering Consultant," a capitalized term that is not defined; the Agreement defines only "Engineering Consultant." Whether they are the same person, and who appoints the certifier, is not stated.

Commitment Percentage is measured against the "aggregate Total Commitment," but Total Commitment is defined as a fixed US$250,000,000 (increasable to US$530,000,000) rather than as the sum of the Lenders' actual commitments. If commitments are cancelled under Section 2.08(a), the percentages need not aggregate to 100% for Required Lender votes.

The definition says the Lenders "become a party" to a Common Project Financing Facility that "may be subject to an Intercreditor Agreement," without stating how or on whose consent that happens. The permissive "may" leaves the pari passu ranking it promises without any enforcement mechanism.

The term sweeps in "the executed documents included by or on behalf of the Borrower in the IntraLinks electronic data site" with no list or index, so what is Confidential Information Material (and hence a Disclosed Matter) cannot be fixed from the instrument. The carve-out proviso further disclaims the very representations the definition otherwise imports.

The proviso lets the Borrower and a counterparty substitute Minnesota or foreign governing law into a Consent and Agreement "without the consent of the Required Lenders or the Security Agent being required," which does not square with the Additional Security Documents and Security Documents definitions requiring security instruments to be satisfactory to the Security Agent. It also sits uneasily with the Section 9.02 amendment machinery for Loan Documents.

"Control" turns on the power to direct "the management or policies of a Person ... by contract or otherwise," a formula with no ownership or voting threshold. Whether a lender's covenant rights or a shareholder agreement confers Control cannot be answered from the words.

"Other assets that are due, or likely to be converted into cash, sold, exchanged, or expensed in the normal course of business, within one (1) year" turns on the vague test "likely," with no probability standard or measurer. Because the Security Agreement subordinates the Lenders' interest in Current Assets to a Working Capital Bank, the boundary matters.

Clause (c) captures "all scheduled amortization repayments of any other Indebtedness" without saying what it is "other" than, given that clause (a) covers finance charges and clause (b) lease principal. The scope of the residual category is left to inference.

"Any matters disclosed in the Confidential Information Material" makes the disclosure exception co-extensive with an undelimited data room and an information memorandum prepared by a third party. What has been disclosed, and therefore excepted from the representations, cannot be determined from the text.

The add-back for "any items treated as exceptional or extraordinary items" does not say by whom they are so treated and, unlike Adjusted Net Income, does not distinguish gains from losses. The same items are already excluded at the Adjusted Net Income stage, so the add-back's operation is uncertain.

The definition points to "the Guarantee Agreement," singular, while the Agreement defines only "Guarantee Agreements" — two separate documents in the forms of Exhibits E-1 and E-2. The release date is in fact defined only in the EGL Guarantee Agreement, and that document conditions it on offtake agreements approved by 66 2/3% of Term Loan Exposure, a standard found nowhere in this Agreement.

A replacement consultant need only be an "independent, professional and reputable engineering firm appointed," without saying who appoints it or on what standard of acceptance. The cross-reference is also left incomplete as "Section 5.04(b".

The Environmental Consultant is simply "such independent, professional and reputable environmental advisory firm appointed," naming no firm and no appointing party. The qualifying adjectives supply no measurable standard.

After naming four specific contracts the definition adds "any other material contract entered into by the Borrower with respect to any engineering, procurement or construction services in connection with the Project." The catch-all uses an undefined materiality test and invites an ejusdem generis dispute about its reach.

The Escrow Account is to receive "all Cash and receivables arising out of any contracts of the Borrower ... or payments otherwise received by Borrower, to be applied in accordance with the Cash Sweep Mechanism," which cannot be squared with Section 2.05, under which the Escrow Agent makes funds available to the Borrower for the purposes in its Borrowing Request. The Cash Sweep Mechanism governs only sweep payments and supplies no application rule for ordinary receipts.

The definition contemplates "any successor collateral agent appointed pursuant to the Collateral Account Agreement," although the collateral agent role belongs to the separately defined Security Agent and no "collateral agent" is defined. The mismatch leaves it unclear whose successor is meant.

The definition says the term "refers to whether such Loan ... are bearing interest at a rate determined by reference to the LIBO Rate," which defines a category by posing a question rather than by fixing a class. It also mismatches singular and plural subjects.

Clause (ii) turns on withholding Tax imposed "under any Laws in effect at the time such recipient acquires its ownership interest," using a capitalized "Laws" that the Agreement never defines. Whether it means only tax laws of a particular jurisdiction is left open.

The definition omits its operative verb: "\"Existing Credit Agreement\" the Credit Agreement dated September 22, 2010 between the Borrower and Union Bank of India." As written it is a fragment rather than a definition.

The FACR numerator counts fixed assets over which the Secured Parties hold a first priority security interest "(subject only to Permitted Liens thereon)", but "Permitted Liens" is not a defined term in this Agreement, which defines "Permitted Encumbrances" instead. The denominator likewise refers to an "Upstream Supplier Project Financing Creditor," a term that appears nowhere else.

Financial Closure requires Total Commitments aggregating US$530,000,000, but the Total Commitment definition fixes the commitment at US$250,000,000 unless Subsequent Project Lenders accede under Section 2.20, which no one is obliged to procure. Availability of Initial Lender Tranche B under Section 2.02(b) and the fixing of the Scheduled Commercial Operations Date both hang on a condition that may be incapable of satisfaction.

The enumerated events close with "or other similar acts beyond the reasonable control of the Borrower," a general catch-all after a list of specifics that raises an ejusdem generis question about its reach. Whether things such as supplier insolvency or regulatory delay qualify is not answerable from the list.

"Related proceedings thereto that may be filed elsewhere in Federal or state court" has no boundary of subject matter, party or time. Because the Great Lakes Litigation is carved out of the representations and defaults, the width of "related proceedings" is consequential.

The definition describes the Guarantee Agreements as guarantees "with respect to the Obligations" without qualification, whereas the EGL Guarantee Agreement actually delivered caps EGL's liability at $250,000,000 after the Commercial Operations Date and terminates on the EGL Guarantee Release Date. Whether the credit agreement's description or the executed guarantee governs the scope of the guarantee is a live question.

"Guarantor" is defined disjunctively as "either of (i) the Parent or (ii) EGL, as the case may be," while the recitals and covenants speak of "the Guarantors" collectively. Whether obligations expressed by reference to "the Guarantor" bind both, and whether they are joint, is not resolved.

Clause (i) captures obligations "in respect of any Working Capital Bank Facility," a capitalized term the Agreement never defines; the defined term is "Working Capital Bank Financing." The mismatch leaves the scope of that limb of Indebtedness uncertain.

This account is to receive insurance, expropriation, asset-sale and equity proceeds, while the Escrow Account definition requires the Borrower to deposit "all Cash and receivables ... or payments otherwise received by Borrower" into the Escrow Account. The two deposit directions overlap and neither yields to the other.

A replacement insurance adviser need only be an "independent, professional and reputable insurance advisory firm appointed," with no appointing party or approval standard identified. The cross-reference is also left incomplete as "Section 5.07(b".

The Intercreditor Agent is appointed "by the Lenders under an Intercreditor Agreement" that, under the Intercreditor Agreement definition, need only be entered into "if and when" the parties agree, yet the Agents definition already treats the Intercreditor Agent as one of the Agents. The office may never come into existence while provisions addressed to the Agents assume it does.

The Intercreditor Agreement must be "in form and substance satisfactory to the Borrower and the Required Lenders," but the Supplier Financing definition states that the Supplier Financing "shall be subject to an Intercreditor Agreement" as a condition of that financing. A document whose existence depends on future agreement is made a precondition to financing already contemplated.

The definition mixes referents: it speaks of "any Eurodollar Rate Borrowing" and then of "the Interest Period applicable to the Borrowing of which such Loan is a part," though no Loan has been introduced. The antecedent failure leaves the payment date for a Loan within a Borrowing to be inferred.

Clause (b) is enumerated "(i) ... and (iii)" with no (ii), and the provisos are then lettered (a), (b) and (c), duplicating the lettering of the definition's own clauses (a) and (b). The broken enumeration makes it unclear what the provisos qualify.

Limb (b) announces "the sum of (i) ... plus the aggregate amount of all LC Disbursements outstanding," omitting the numeral (ii) and thereby blurring whether the second amount is Lender-specific or facility-wide. Read with limb (a)(ii) the same LC Disbursements may be counted twice.

"Lender" includes "any assignee ... that becomes a Project Lender pursuant to an Assignment and Assumption," but "Project Lender" is a recital term embracing suppliers' credit providers as well as term lenders. An assignee under Section 9.04 becomes a Lender, not a Project Lender, so the two definitions do not fit.

This definition fixes the share as of the date the Borrower must prepay "in accordance with Section 2.11(b)," while the Cash Sweep Mechanism directs prepayment "pro rata to each Lender in accordance with its Lender's Pro Rata Interest in accordance with Section 2.11(c)(vii)." The two provisions point to different prepayment provisions for the same calculation.

The definition caps expiry at the earlier of 36 months from issuance and four years from the date of the Agreement (December 29, 2014), yet clause (4) permits negotiation of a letter of credit up to December 30, 2014 — a day after the outer expiry. The internal dates cannot all be satisfied.

The fallback applies only "In the event that such rate is not available at the time of determination for any other Interest Period," so on its face no fallback exists for the Interest Period actually being priced. The stray word "other" defeats the substitute-rate mechanism.

The list of Loan Documents ends with "any other document designated from time to time as a Loan Document by the Lenders or the Facility Agent," allowing unilateral expansion of a defined category that carries covenants, defaults and cross-default consequences. The general catch-all stands against the enumerated specifics with no consent requirement.

Long-Term Debt excludes installments due within one year from clauses (b) and (c) but not from clause (a), while Short-Term Debt separately includes "installments on Long-Term Debt due within one (1) year." The two definitions overlap on the same amounts and Total Debt then adds them together.

Clause (ii) turns on the Reuters "LIBOO1" screen rate, whereas the LIBO Rate definition prices off the Reuters "LIBOR01" screen. The disruption test and the rate definition refer to different pages, so it is unclear which screen governs.

"Material adverse effect on the business, financial condition, operations or performance or properties of the Borrower since March 31, 2010" supplies no measure of materiality and fixes an arbitrary baseline date predating the Agreement. What change qualifies, and against what benchmark, is left entirely open.

"All material approvals and consents by any Person, including any Governmental Authority, required in connection with the Project" combines an undefined materiality test with an open-ended "including, but not limited to" list. The Schedule 4.01(f) enumeration does not limit the term.

Limb (ii) brings in "any and all mining rights and leases of the Borrower with acknowledgment from the relevant Government Authorities or other Person which is a lessor consenting to such Mortgage," so mining leases are Mortgaged Property only if a third party consents. Whether unconsented mining leases are within the collateral is left unresolved by the words used.

Clause (ii)(B) credits amounts "deposited at such time in the DSRA, the Escrow Account or the Unrestricted Account established in accordance with the Collateral Account Agreement," but "Unrestricted Account" is used as a defined term and is nowhere defined in the Agreement. The arithmetic of clause (i) is also garbled — "minus, (B) ... and (C) minus mark-to-market amounts ... that ... are less than twenty five million Dollars."

Clause (iii) deducts taxes "including, in the case of any such event in respect of any Foreign Subsidiary, taxes payable upon the repatriation of such proceeds to the United States," though "Foreign Subsidiary" is undefined and the Subsidiary definition records that the Borrower has no Subsidiary. The limb has no possible application as drafted.

The definition of "Obligations" is circular, ending each limb "in each case to the extent arising in connection with the Obligations." Because the Guarantee Agreements define Borrower Obligations by reference to this term, the limitation's meaning cannot be fixed from its own words.

"Obligor" means "any of the Borrowers or any Guarantor," using a plural "Borrowers" although the Agreement defines a single "Borrower." The mismatch leaves it unclear whether some other entity was intended to be captured.

"Each of the operative contracts and agreements entered into by the Borrower for the sale of goods and products" gives no test of what makes a sales contract "operative," and excludes only spot sales payable within forty-five days. Whether a term sheet, framework or rolling sales arrangement is an Offtake Contract is not determinable.

The permitted purpose is capital expenditure "for de-bottlenecking and other similar performance and operational and efficiency enhancing modifications to the Project," a general phrase following a single specific with no boundary. Whether an expansion or replacement of plant qualifies is left to argument.

The closing proviso reads "the term \"Permitted Encumbrances\" shall not include any Lien securing Indebtedness on Attributable Debt," which is ungrammatical and leaves it unclear whether the carve-out covers Liens securing Indebtedness or Attributable Debt or only some combination. The exception list — clauses (e), (h), (j) and (p) — turns on that same broken phrase.

Clause (e) permits "repurchase agreements ... with a maturity not less than one (1) year thereafter," the reverse of the short-maturity limits imposed by clauses (a) through (d). Read literally, only long-dated repos qualify, which contradicts the liquidity purpose of the definition.

The opening words require the Required Lenders' prior written consent for any material change in the scope of works, while the second proviso says that consent "shall not be required" for de-bottlenecking and similar modifications financed from equity, promoter loans or the Unrestricted Account. The two cannot both be applied to a debottlenecking change that is material in scope.

The sentence is broken: "includes any Permitted Project Change subject to the receipt of approval, if any, required in the definition of Permitted Project Change has been approved as set forth in the definition of that term." As written it is unclear whether an unapproved change is nevertheless part of the Project.

The stacked provisos leave it unclear whether sub-threshold contracts and Schedule 1.01E contracts are excluded from "Project Contracts" generally or only "for purposes of requiring the Borrower to provide a Consent and Agreement," with a further redefinition for Sections 6.09 and 6.10. The same term therefore carries different scopes in different places without a governing rule.

"Project Lender" takes its meaning from the recitals, where it embraces suppliers' credit providers as well as the Initial Lender and Subsequent Project Lenders, whereas the operative Lender definition treats an assignee as becoming a "Project Lender." The recital-sourced term and the operative term do not describe the same class.

"The date specified in the financial Covenants" assumes Section 6.12 specifies testing dates for every ratio, and supplies no default if it does not. The lower-case "financial" also leaves it uncertain whether the defined term "Financial Covenants" is intended.

The definition gives two different periods — (a) each fiscal year and (b) each rolling half-year straddling two fiscal years — without saying which applies to which covenant or whether both apply at once. Any ratio tested "for a Relevant Period" therefore has two possible measuring periods.

Required Lenders act by a 51% threshold, but the EGL Guarantee Agreement conditions the EGL Guarantee Release Date on offtake agreements acceptable to Lenders holding not less than 66 2/3% of Term Loan Exposure. Which lender-consent standard governs decisions touching the guarantee is not reconciled.

The list of Responsible Officers — "chief executive officer, president, general manager, the treasurer, the chief financial officer, the general counsel or any vice president" — is a closed enumeration of corporate titles applied to a Minnesota limited liability company managed by governors and managers. Whether a manager or governor can certify is not answered.
The proviso excludes "any Tax Distribution," a singular term the Agreement never defines; the defined term is "Tax Distributions." The mismatch leaves the carve-out's reference uncertain.

The date is "mutually determined by the Required Lenders and the Borrower at the time of Financial Closure," so if Financial Closure (which requires US$530,000,000 of commitments) never occurs, no date is ever set, even though the backstop of June 30, 2013 and the Force Majeure and First Sweep Period definitions depend on it. The definition cannot be operated independently of the Financial Closure definition.

"Secured Party" lists only the Lenders, the Issuing Banks and the Upstream Supplier Financing Creditors, omitting the Security Agent and Facility Agent, although the Security Agent definition says it acts "as security agent for the Secured Parties" and the Collateral definition speaks of Liens granted in favour of the Secured Parties. EPIL, the actual lender of the Supplier Financing, is likewise not included.

The definition says the Borrower grants "a first perfected security interest in the Collateral ... including all assets and properties," then provides that the interest in Current Assets "will be junior to the security interest of any lender under the Working Capital Bank Financing." The grant cannot be both first and junior over the same assets.

The definition opens with "any Person (other than an Affiliate of the Borrower) that agrees, following the date of this Agreement ... to become a party hereto as a Lender," then parenthetically includes "an existing Lender that increases its Commitment Percentage," who is already a party. It also requires consent of "the Facility Agent and the Lenders" for non-bank accedents, a unanimity standard that departs from the Required Lenders standard used elsewhere.

The definition embeds a factual representation — "the Borrower has no Subsidiary" — for purposes of the representations and conditions to borrowing, duplicating and potentially conflicting with Section 3.12 (Subsidiaries) and Section 5.12. Whether a breach of that statement is a misrepresentation under Article III or merely a definitional assumption is unclear.

Supplier Financing is capped at "one hundred eighty three million Dollars (US$183,000,000)" in the aggregate, while the Financial Closure definition conditions closure on Supplier Financing "in an aggregate amount equal to one hundred eighty two million seven hundred fifty thousand Dollars (US$182,750,000)." The two figures for the same financing do not match.

The availability period ends September 30, 2013, yet Section 2.06(a) permits Letters of Credit to be issued to June 30, 2013 with expiries up to December 29, 2014, and Section 2.06(e) converts any later LC Disbursement automatically into a Term Loan. Term Loans can therefore arise after the availability period has lapsed and the commitments have terminated.

The last sentence is broken — "shall be set forth or in the Assignment and Assumption or Accession Agreement" — leaving unclear whether some other place of record was intended. It also does not say which document controls if both exist for the same Lender.

The Term Loan Maturity Date is fixed at January 1, 2020, a date that can never be a Business Day under the Business Day definition, while Section 2.09 requires the final installment to be paid "on the Term Loan Maturity Date." The date definition and the payment mechanics do not fit together.

Total Commitment is fixed at US$250,000,000, increasable only by Accession Agreements, yet the Financial Closure definition requires Total Commitments to equal US$530,000,000 and the recitals describe term lending of that amount. The definition cannot deliver the aggregate the rest of the Agreement assumes.

Clause (b) adds "Short-Term Debt and Working Capital Bank Finance," using a term the Agreement never defines; the defined term is "Working Capital Bank Financing." Since Short-Term Debt already subtracts Working Capital Bank Financing, the undefined addition also risks double counting.

Limb (b) defines "Transactions" to include "the completion and operations of the Project and any matters related thereto," a boundless category that then feeds Transaction Costs and the representations made with respect to the Transactions. What is "related thereto" cannot be delimited from the text.

The definition restricts payments to amounts "in the Unrestricted Account," a capitalized term that is used here and in the Net Debt and Permitted Project Change definitions but is never defined in the Agreement. The only permitted source of repayment is therefore an undefined account.

The definition names a closed class — "namely, the Export-Import Bank of India and the Central Bank of India" — while also describing generically "the providers of supplier financing to EPIL." Whether another upstream financier can ever become an Upstream Supplier Financing Creditor is left to an expressio unius argument.

The closing condition is ungrammatical — "require a mandatory prepayment ... on the same terms as the required by the Loans" — and does not say whether it qualifies only limb (b)(iii) or the whole fraction. The composition of the denominator, and hence the creditor's share, turns on that unresolved reading.

Section 1.03 requires all terms "of an accounting or financial nature" to be construed in accordance with GAAP, yet defined financial terms such as Cash Available and Adjusted Tangible Net Worth are built on non-GAAP concepts like "standalone net profits after taxation" and "bad or doubtful expenses not provided for." Which controls when the defined formula departs from GAAP is not addressed.

Section 2.01 says the undrawn Term Loan Commitment "shall lapse automatically at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period" and that no Term Loan may exceed a Lender's Unused Commitment, but Section 2.06(e) converts LC Disbursements into Term Loans automatically whenever they occur, including after that date. The lapse rule and the automatic conversion cannot both operate.

Tranche B availability extends to "any remaining amount of the Initial Lender Tranche A Total Commitment to the extent not previously borrowed," whereas Section 2.02(a)(ii) makes that same remaining Tranche A amount available only on satisfaction of the Section 4.02 conditions. The Tranche A remainder is subject to two different condition sets.

The proviso that "no proceeds shall be used to fund or maintain the DSRA" cannot be squared with Section 2.06(j), under which amounts paid on an Event of Default are deposited into the DSRA "as supplemental to the Required Amount," and with the Section 5.15 obligation to fund the DSRA. The permitted-use restriction and the funding obligations pull in opposite directions.

The Borrower's discretion to request non-ratable Loans is made "subject to Section 2.03(c)," which deals only with Eurodollar Rate Borrowings and funding through branches, not with allocation or size; the minimum-amount and number limits sit in Section 2.03(d). The internal cross-reference appears to point to the wrong subsection.

"Each Borrowing shall be comprised entirely of Eurodollar Rate Borrowings" defines a Borrowing by reference to Borrowings, and under the Borrowing definition a Borrowing may be an LC Exposure, which bears no LIBO-based Interest Period. The sentence cannot be applied to every Borrowing as defined.

"In not more than fifteen (15) Borrowings" does not say whether the cap runs per Lender, per tranche or across the whole facility, or what happens to a request that would exceed it. The minimum-amount carve-out for the balance of an Unused Commitment compounds the uncertainty.

The section provides that if a Eurodollar Rate Borrowing is unavailable under Section 2.14 "the Lenders may make the requested Borrowing ... but they shall have no obligation to do so," which cannot be squared with Section 2.01 and Section 2.03(b), under which the Lenders' several Term Loan Commitments are binding obligations to fund. A market-disruption event would convert a committed facility into a discretionary one.

This section requires the Escrow Agent to make funds "available to the Borrower for the purposes specified by the Borrower in its applicable Borrowing Request," while the Escrow Account definition says amounts in that account are "to be applied in accordance with the Cash Sweep Mechanism as set forth in the Collateral Account Agreement." The two release regimes for the same account are not reconciled.

The section makes issuance subject to "the applicable limitations on the Initial Lender Tranche A Commitment set forth in Section 2.02(a)," a term that is not defined; the defined terms are Initial Lender Tranche A and Initial Lender Tranche A Total Commitment. Which limit constrains letter of credit issuance is therefore uncertain.

The documentary requirements are enumerated in five specific alternatives and then closed with "(vi) such other documents as may be specified by the Issuing Bank from time to time." That open catch-all after a specific list leaves the Borrower's condition to satisfaction indeterminate.

This expiration rule (the earlier of 36 months from issuance and four years from the date of the Agreement, i.e. December 29, 2014) sits against the Letter of Credit definition, which allows issuance up to June 30, 2013 and negotiation "not later than December 30, 2014." A letter of credit negotiated on the last permitted day would already have expired.

Automatic conversion of every LC Disbursement into a Term Loan takes no account of the limit in Section 2.01 that a Term Loan arising by automatic conversion "shall not exceed the Unused Commitment of such Lender," nor of the lapse of commitments at the end of the Term Loan Availability Period. The conversion mechanic and the commitment limits conflict.

The section preserves the Issuing Bank's liability for direct damages "caused by such Issuing Bank's failure to exercise care when determining whether drafts and other documents presented ... comply," and then deems care to have been exercised absent gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud. The saving proviso and the deeming sentence largely cancel each other.

This paragraph gives the Issuing Bank "the final word" on documentary compliance and bars the Borrower from questioning it absent gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud, which cannot be squared with Section 2.06(f)'s preservation of liability for a failure to exercise care in examining documents. The two paragraphs set different standards for the same decision.

The Borrower "grants the Lenders a security interest in all funds and investments in such account," whereas under the Security Agreement and Security Documents definitions all Liens are granted to the Security Agent for the ratable benefit of the holders of the Secured Obligations. Who holds the cash collateral security, and for whom, is inconsistent across the instrument.

The subsection enumerates "(i) ... and (iii)" with no clause (ii), reproducing the same broken enumeration as the Interest Period definition. It is unclear whether a provision was dropped from the election mechanics.

The subsection lets Lenders cancel Unused Commitments "upon prior written notice to the Borrower ... immediately upon such notice ... for any reason," and then says that except where cancellation is due to credit deterioration the Lenders "shall endeavor to provide prior notice." The mandatory prior-notice requirement and the best-efforts notice sentence contradict each other.

The Borrower's right to reduce commitments arises only "if the Project costs shall have been reduced below one billion ninety seven million Dollars (US$1,097,000,000)" — a figure that appears only as a current estimate in the recitals. Whether that recital estimate fixes the operative benchmark, and who measures the reduction, is left open.

The proviso that payments falling on a non-Business Day be made "on the next preceding Business Day" cannot be squared with the further proviso that the final installment "shall be paid on the Term Loan Maturity Date," which is January 1, 2020 and can never be a Business Day. The two provisos give different dates for the last payment.
